In nineteen eighteen, a magazine for baby stores said: pink is for boys, blue is for girls. And it gave a reason. Pink is a stronger, more decided color, so it suits a boy. Blue is delicate and dainty, so it's prettier for a girl. The same logic we use today, used for the exact opposite. The colors never meant anything. The meaning was attached by whoever was selling. Made to Want.

Until about a hundred years ago, little boys wore white dresses. Look at any family photo from the eighteen hundreds. Every small child is in white. There's a famous photo of two year old Franklin Roosevelt in a white dress, with long hair. White was practical. You could boil it and bleach it, and pass it down to the next child, boy or girl. Boys got their first trousers at six or seven, with a haircut. Almost a ceremony. Until then, a baby was just a baby. Made to Want.

In nineteen twenty seven, Time magazine asked America's biggest stores: which color is for boys? Filene's in Boston said pink. So did Marshall Field's in Chicago. Other stores said the opposite. So you buy a pink outfit for your son in Chicago, and a store in another city tells you that you got it backwards. There was no rule. Just stores, and each store had a guess. Made to Want.

Baby clothes split into pink and blue because of prenatal tests. In the nineteen seventies, unisex clothes had almost won. Then, in the nineteen eighties, parents could learn if it was a boy or a girl months before the birth. That gave stores something new to sell: time. Neutral clothes started to disappear. Blue got a football. Pink got a bow and a kitten. Then strollers, bottles, bedding, wallpaper. The more you split it, the more you can sell. Made to Want.

The pink version often costs more. It even has a name: the pink tax. In twenty fifteen, New York City compared nearly eight hundred products sold in a men's and a women's version. The women's version cost about seven percent more on average. Often it was the exact same item, just in a different color. And a pink stroller is hard to hand down to a little brother. So a lot of families end up buying everything twice. Made to Want.

The gender reveal party is younger than the iPhone. It started in two thousand eight. An American mother cut into a cake, and the inside was pink. She posted about it online. Now it's a whole industry of balloons, smoke cannons and confetti, all built on one question: pink or blue? A hundred years ago, the answer would have been backwards. In nineteen eighteen, pink was for boys. Made to Want.
